title: The NSF Seafood Engine in New England Wins $15M Award to Strengthen Fisheries and Aquaculture - University of New Hampshire
content: The U.S. National Science Foundation (NSF) announced a major new award to bolster the American seafood industry through the NSF Regional Innovation Engines (NSF Engines) program within the Directorate for Technology, Innovation, and Partnerships (NSF TIP). The NSF Seafood Engine in New England, led by the Portsmouth-based non-profit NERACOOS, is a collaboration of seafood industry, tech sector, government, and research partners across Maine, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, and Rhode Island, including UNH. This innovation ecosystem aims to revitalize the seafood sector through cutting-edge technology. This award will position New England to lead the nation in meeting the goals outlined in the Executive Order on Restoring American Seafood Competitiveness. “New Hampshire may only have about 18 miles of coastline, but we benefit tremendously from the seafood industry and our coastal economy,” says New Hampshire Sen. Jeanne Shaheen. “I’m thankful the National Science Foundation recognized those benefits and also the immense potential of the maritime economy by selecting the Seafood Engine in New England as a new NSF Engine. This award will provide the resources to make the engine a success, strengthening fisheries and aquaculture throughout New England, creating good jobs, promoting innovation and boosting our competitiveness in the world.” The Seafood Engine will initially receive an award of $15 million over two years, with the potential to grow up to $160 million over 10 years as it works to build an internationally competitive technology and innovation cluster. This core funding from NSF creates an unprecedented opportunity to leverage additional resources from public, private, and philanthropic sources to expand the partnership and scale its outcomes. The NSF Engine strives to enhance the competitiveness of fisheries and aquaculture, a pillar of New England's economy that accounts for 25% of the nation’s seafood value. The technological solutions can be rolled out nationwide, propelling the American seafood industry to a stronger position within the global market. “Built on the ingenuity and steadfast determination at the heart of America’s oldest commercial enterprise, the Seafood Engine is ready to confront key challenges facing the industry with bold innovation,” says Jake Kritzer, principal investigator of the Seafood Engine and executive director of NERACOOS. Support an exciting portfolio of R&D projects that bring together seafood harvesters, academic experts, and tech companies aimed at building ocean intelligence through state-of-the-art sensors deployed from fishing vessels and aquaculture farms. Form a consortium of regional seafood apprenticeship programs at the center of the Engine’s Workforce Development strategy through which new entrants can participate in R&D projects and operationalize their innovations. Provide funding to blue tech companies that have passed the R&D phase and need support to bring products to commercialization through the Translation of Innovation to Impact strategy. Over time, new R&D, Workforce Development, and Translation activities will work to reshore American seafood processing capacity and strengthen the full supply chain. Together, these efforts will bring new opportunities to small and medium firms across the New England coastline and cut into the $20 billion seafood deficit facing American businesses. "UNH is proud to be a partner in the effort to bring technological innovation to one of New England’s most important heritage industries,” UNH President Elizabeth Chilton says. “This public-private partnership will strengthen our seafood supply chain and bolster coastal communities across the region.” In early summer 2024, the Seafood Engine submitted one of nearly 300 letters of intent in response to the second NSF Engines funding opportunity. The preliminary proposal was selected as one of 71 to advance to the next round of competition. Following a merit review, the Seafood Engine was one of 29 teams to share a detailed presentation about their proposed NSF Engine. From this process, 15 finalists were selected to participate in two-day site visits with NSF staff and external experts. The Seafood Engine is one of 12 NSF Engines award winners selected from among these finalists. Copyright © 2026 , University of New Hampshire. All rights reserved.

title: UNH Vs. HUM: Which Insurer Stock Has More Upside After CMS Reverses Wall Street’s Biggest Medicare Rate Fear? - Stocktwits
content: Shares of UnitedHealth, Inc. (UNH) and Humana, Inc. (HUM) are back in the spotlight on Tuesday after the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) lifted Medicare Advantage payment rates for 2027, with Wall Street estimates pointing to a clear frontrunner. UNH stock rose 8% in extended trading, while HUM stock gained 11%. Over the past year, however, UNH has fallen about 45% and HUM nearly 27%, with both stocks underperforming the broader Health Care Select Sector SPDR Fund (XLV), which climbed 10% over the same period. The CMS finalized a 2.48% increase in Medicare Advantage payment rates for 2027, up from the January proposal that kept rates roughly flat and wiped out nearly $100 billion in market value across major insurers. The updated policy is expected to add more than $13 billion in additional funding to Medicare Advantage plans next year, the CMS said. With the policy overhang removed, attention has shifted back to valuation targets, which point to higher implied upside for UnitedHealth than for Humana. Based on Koyfin estimates, UnitedHealth carries a 12-month average price target of $357.81, implying a 27% upside from the stock’s last close. Coverage across 29 analysts includes 7 ‘Strong Buy’, 16 ‘Buy’, 4 ‘Hold’ and 2 ‘Sell’ ratings. Earlier this month, Raymond James upgraded the stock to ‘Outperform’ with a $330 price target, citing potential upside from expense trends and expected margin improvement at Optum Health, the company’s care delivery arm. Meanwhile, Bernstein SocGen Group reiterated an ‘Outperform’ rating with a $405 target, pointing to UnitedHealth’s expanding AI strategy. The company recently launched its generative AI companion, Avery, as part of broader efforts to reduce operating costs across its insurance segment, where it plans nearly $1 billion in expense cuts and is closing or divesting about 550 Optum Health clinics. UnitedHealth also expects to lose as many as 2.8 million insurance members this year, with revenue potentially declining for the first time since the 1980s as longtime chair and former CEO Stephen Hemsley leads a turnaround effort. The stock still remains below the level at which Warren Buffett’s Berkshire Hathaway built its stake last year and faces scrutiny over Medicare Advantage risk-adjustment practices following a Senate committee review. Humana’s upside appears more modest based on Koyfin estimates, with a 12-month average price target of $212.17, implying a 16% upside from current levels. Among 27 covering analysts, the stock carries 2 ‘Strong Buy’, 6 ‘Buy’, 17 ‘Hold’ and 2 ‘Sell’ ratings. Earlier this year, the company projected adjusted 2026 earnings of at least $9 per share, below consensus expectations of $11.87, while the insurer said margins in its individual Medicare Advantage business could remain just below break-even this year. Several brokerages subsequently lowered price targets, with UBS and BofA maintaining ‘Neutral’ ratings after Humana’s 2026 EPS outlook came in roughly 24% below consensus. On the other hand, Morgan Stanley warned that uncertainty around the size of Humana’s 2026 membership cohort remains a risk “particularly heading into 2027 and beyond.” Cantor Fitzgerald said the stock may remain range-bound until clearer membership data emerges in the second quarter, and Guggenheim said it was taking “a prudent view” of the company’s 2027 earnings outlook. Still, Humana expects enrollment in its individual Medicare Advantage plans to increase about 25% in 2026 compared with last year, with over 70% of new members coming from competing plans. As of 10.15 p.m. ET, Nasdaq 100 futures were down 0.8%, while S&P 500 futures were down by 0.6%. Dow futures were down 0.4%. He said negotiations were “going well,” but added that restoring access through Hormuz remains a “very big priority.” He also said that while he would like the U.S. to “take the oil,” Americans ultimately want U.S. forces to return home. Morgan Asset & Wealth Management, said that the belief the U.S. economy is insulated from a closure of the Strait of Hormuz is “mostly false,” adding that U.S. fossil-fuel independence “is not as much of an economic firewall as you might think.” In the previous session, the S&P 500 logged its fourth straight session of gains, marking its longest winning streak since January: Investors also weighed weaker-than-expected economic data, with the U.S. services sector expanding at a slower pace in March. title: UNH crews search Lake Massabesic for missing WWII B-17 ball turret - UnionLeader.com

Research project manager Andy McLeod prepares to launch the University of New Hampshire’s autonomous mapping boat to search for remnants of a World War II-era B-17 Flying Fortress at the bottom of Lake Massabesic in late June. University of New Hampshire student Ashley Riz Advincula watches the monitors in a research trailer as and autonomous mapping boat searches for remnants of a World War II-ear B-17 Flying Fortress in Lake Massabesic. Historian Dennis Sasseville speaks with a reporter about the search for remnants of a World War II-ear B-17 Flying Fortress in Lake Massabesic. Research project manager Andy McLeod holds up the one of the remotes for the University of New Hampshire’s autonomous mapping boat as it sets sail to search for remnants of a World War II-ear B-17 Flying Fortress in Lake Massabesic late last month. Research project manager Andy McLeod, left, and University of New Hampshire student Tion Uriam prepare to launch an autonomous mapping boat to search for remnants of a World War II-ear B-17 Flying Fortress at Lake Massabesic. A rare copy of the Declaration of Independence found a new home after South Jers… Tuskegee Airman veteran Howard Carter, who proudly served in the Korean War and … Research project manager Andy McLeod with the Center for Coastal and Ocean Mapping / Joint Hydrographic Center from the University of New Hampshire - Chase Ocean Engineering Lab and UNH student Tion Uriam (right) do a final check before launching a yellow battery powered uncrewed (robotic) surface vessel (USV), as it heads out to search Lake Massabesic for a ball gun turret dumped off a WWII B-17 Flying Fortress and into the water below following an aborted landing attempt at Grenier Air Base (known today as Manchester-Boston Regional Airport) in January 1945. Living near Lake Massabesic, Alex Saidel grew up hearing stories of the history lying somewhere below the surface. “I always heard there was either a World War II plane or parts here or something like that, but that was always the end of it,” said Saidel, an aviation buff and president of Merrimack Street Volvo. “But what if we can find it?” Over the past few weeks, teams from the Center for Coastal & Ocean Mapping/Joint Hydrographic Center, based at the University of New Hampshire’s Chase Ocean Engineering Lab were at Lake Massabesic, working with Saidel while searching for a ball gun turret from a B-17 Flying Fortress. The turret was jettisoned from the bomber following an aborted landing attempt during a training flight out of Grenier Air Base — known today as Manchester-Boston Regional Airport — in January 1945. Crews hope to find and raise the turret to the surface using cables and flotation devices, tow it to shore and restore it for display in the Aviation Museum of N.H. “Today, almost no physical trace remains of Grenier Air Base, which once housed thousands of troops from all over the nation as they trained for missions in Europe and all over the world,” said Jeff Rapsis, the museum’s executive director. “Displaying the ball turret would provide Aviation Museum visitors a tangible connection to Grenier Air Base and Manchester’s role during World War II.” The story of this search begins not 60 feet below the surface of Manchester’s drinking water source, but in a car dealership. When Dennis Sasseville — a local historian and aviation history enthusiast — showed up at Saidel’s Volvo dealership, as luck would have it, the salesmen were busy with other customers, and Saidel assisted him with finding a car for him and his wife. Sasseville himself was familiar with the story of a B-17 ball turret in Lake Massabesic after reading a mention of it in author Ed Brouder’s book, “Manchester’s Airport: Flying Through Time.” “I said, in the era of internet let’s do some more research. So, I found that there was an accident report,” Sasseville said. “At that time you could send away to a database for $25 or $30 and get the actual photocopies of the Army accident report. I did that and did a little bit more research, and over the years I would tell fellow amateur historians about it, and most of them kind of shrugged their shoulders and said, ‘Well, that’s nice.’” When it came time to put pen to paper on his car purchase, Sasseville noticed a lot of World War II memorabilia in Saidel’s office. “We get talking about World War II and he’s actually flown a restored B-17,” Sasseville said. “I said, ‘Well you know there’s this ball turret in Massabesic Lake’ and his eyes just lit up.” He reached out to the University of New Hampshire, and the hunt was on. Since about mid-June, engineers and experts from UNH have been focused on locating the ball turret from the B‑17 aircraft (serial number 44-6694). The plane, which belonged to the 99th Bombardment Group, was reportedly en route to Tortorella Air Base in Foggia, Italy, when the gun turret was intentionally dropped into the lake after a failed landing attempt at Grenier Field. The tailwheel broke off, making a second landing attempt dangerous. The B-17 ball turret is affixed to the underside of the fuselage in a way that could break the back of the fuselage when touching down without landing gear (dubbed a belly landing). According to the accident report, the pilot was told to “Drop the turret into the lake.” Working with staff from Manchester Water Works, UNH crews set up a mobile control van along the shore of the lake. From there, they operated a battery-powered, robotic uncrewed surface vessel (USV) outfitted with a M3 Multibeam Echosounder — on loan from KONGSBERG, one of the university’s industry partners — to assist with the exploration efforts. A small Garmin side-scan sonar provided acoustic “imagery” of the lakebed. The advanced high-resolution multibeam sonar allowed the team to collect data for 3D topographic maps, while the Garmin side-scan provided acoustic shadows of objects that could be the turret. Inside the trailer, graduate students in UNH’s summer hydrographic field course took part in the search, giving them a unique opportunity to explore a local body of water for a historical artifact. The class is composed of graduate students from the United States and around the world enrolled at the center, recognized as the nation’s premier Category A Hydrographic mapping training program. Val Schmidt, principal research project manager and UNH team lead, said work like this on an inland lake is new for him. “My office has been this picnic table for the last two weeks. It’s been terrific,” Schmidt said. “We do a lot of stuff off the coast as part of the class and for different things. So it’s not uncommon offshore, but I don’t know of another project that we’ve done in a lake.” Professor Semme Dijkstra, a UNH research scientist at the School of Marine Sciences and Ocean Engineering, said the school is training graduate students from across the U.S. and the world to survey the ocean floor. This year’s class has 10 students. Schmidt said each weekday morning students and staff have been coming out to the trailer near the Water Works Treatment Plant off Lake Shore Road, setting up, having a morning meeting and mapping the lake bed while looking for anything that might be the turret. “They come with a plan about what they want to do for the day and we help them execute it,” Schmidt said. That plan typically involves deploying the boat around 9:30 a.m., launching what Schmidt calls a lawnmower survey because it travels back and forth along equally spaced lines across the lake. A University of New Hampshire autonomous mapping boat searches for remnants of a World War II-ear B-17 Flying Fortress in Lake Massabesic. “They’ve laid out a strategy of where they think the turret is most likely to be, so they’re prioritizing those spots and trying to get full coverage,” Schmidt said. “They program the boat by drawing these lines out on a map and then they can push a button and the boat will just go and run them. Then they monitor the data collection effort as it’s coming in and try to pick out targets or things that we want to go investigate later.” At the end of a wooden dock, research project manager Andy McLeod and UNH student Tion Uriam did a final check on the yellow USV before the day’s run began. “This is a fairly new machine for us, and generally speaking we can do about six to eight hours of ops,” McLeod said. Have their efforts raised any eyebrows among neighbors or folks out on the water? “Maybe the loons, but I haven’t seen anybody come over and get all upset about us,” he said. Back in the trailer, Roland Arsenault — the vehicle’s chief software engineer, monitored a mosaic of camera images tiled across two large monitors. “That’s our side-scan sonar on the left,” Arsenault said. “This is water column, like your fish-finder-type sonar on the right. Here is the map that we use to navigate the boat to plan our missions and to see where we are. And these are the cameras — the boat has four cameras, forward, sides and rear.” Lake Massabesic has a storage capacity of approximately 15 billion gallons of water and covers 2,400 acres, or about four square miles. The lake averages only about 17 feet in depth across its entirety, with the deepest area checking in at approximately 60 feet near Front Park by the Massabesic Yacht Club. Schmidt said the team worked with Alex and Dennis to come up with areas of the lake to focus on. “Just thinking about what you would do if you were a pilot — you probably didn’t want to get near the trees, you don’t want to hit houses or the shoreline. The accident report from the Air Force — there’s very little detail in there about where they were exactly, and where they dropped it and what their strategy was when they dropped it,” Schmidt said. Research project manager Andy McLeod holds up the one of the remotes for the University of New Hampshire’s autonomous mapping boat as it sets sail to search for remnants of a World War II-ear B-17 Flying Fortress in Lake Massabesic late last month. According to the Army Air Force’s accident report, at the time of the accident, “the runways were covered with patches of ice and braking action was fair.” “Due to this condition the pilot of this aircraft made his approach so as to land as short as possible,” the report says. “In doing so his main gear made contact with a snow bank. Seeing what had happened the pilot pulled back on the stick in order to go around again and this caused the tail to be forced down, hitting the snow bank with sufficient force to shear off the tail wheel.” In his statement on the accident, 2nd Lt. Douglas E. Sherman (the pilot) wrote that the tower instructed him and other crew members to “fly over to a lake 4 or 5 miles to jettison the ball turret.” “We went over to the lake and circled while the crew loosened it up,” Sherman wrote. “As soon as the tower instructed us to let it go, we were flying at 1,000 (feet) around two lakes, so we wouldn’t go over any houses. When it left, we were over the lake and I went in. We called the tower and told them the turret was gone and we proceeded back to the field for a wheel landing.” Alex Saidel’s research shows B-17 #44-6694 was originally delivered to Nashville, Tennessee, on Oct. 15, 1944. From there she went to Hunter Army Air Base in Savannah, Georgia, arriving Dec. 8, 1944, before flying to Grenier Field on Jan. 4, 1945, where she was assigned to the 416th Bomb Squadron of the 99th Bombing Group. After dropping the ball turret, the B‑17 aircraft was repaired and sent to Tortorella Air Base in Foggia, Italy, on Feb. 11, 1945, before ultimately taking part in 36 missions between Feb. 22, 1945, and April 26, 1945. The aircraft survived the war and was retired to Bradley Field in Connecticut on July 15, 1945. She was then sent to Independence Airfield in Kansas on July 17, 1945, before being sent to a scrap yard at Kingman, Arizona, on Dec. 21, 1945. The tale of the turret isn’t the only well-worn New Hampshire-based yarn involving a World War II aircraft. Hikers can view the scattered wreckage of a Douglas B-18 Bolo Bomber at Mount Waternomee in Woodstock. The aircraft crashed into the mountain on Jan. 14, 1942, during a blizzard. Five of the seven crew members survived after being rescued by residents of Woodstock and Lincoln. As of this writing, the missing ball turret hasn’t turned up, though Rapsis said the search itself is just as important as finding the relic. “History has so much to teach us, and not just in books,” Rapsis said. “It can be found all around us — sometimes under water. Even if the effort to retrieve the ball turret is ultimately unsuccessful, the search for it is a reminder that all those who answered the call to serve their country in World War II should not be forgotten.” Share your opinion with New Hampshire.
